blocks.text: A **financial market** is the whole infrastructure that lets people trade **financial securities**: currency, bonds, stocks, derivatives, commodities, forex and so on. Buying or selling shares happens in a financial market; so does trading in forex, derivatives or commodities. Banks, insurance companies, mutual funds and pension trusts are also participants. The market makes **efficient trade of securities and transfer of funds** between lenders and borrowers possible, and it creates the securities that people invest in to earn a return.

blocks.title: One-stop shop
blocks.text: Without a financial market, a lender in Mumbai would have to hunt for a borrower in Delhi on her own. The market becomes a **one-stop shop** for all lenders and borrowers, which makes capital generation and investment efficient.

blocks.title: The three roles
rows: Those with **surplus funds**. They invest in securities. Households, businesses and government can all be lenders.
Those in need of funds, or **in capital deficit**. They borrow through the market and its intermediaries. Business, government and households can all be borrowers.

Agencies in an assisting role. They collect funds from lenders, pass capital to borrowers and handle securities (stocks, mutual fund units, bonds, deposit certificates) on their behalf. Examples: banks, brokers, custodians, depositories and depository participants.

blocks.text: Without intermediaries the market cannot run smoothly and efficiently. Financial institutions, mutual funds, insurance companies and pension trusts also act as lenders and intermediaries in the process.

blocks.title: Why a market is needed
items: Without one, lenders and borrowers can only find each other by **self-search**, which is inefficient.
Many lenders and borrowers would **miss the chance** to invest or borrow.
Such an economy is not friendly to economic activity.
An efficient market is an effective source of **capital generation and investment**.

sections.title: Structure: money market and capital market

blocks.text: Most trading happens in two main types of financial market: the **money market** for **short-term** borrowing and lending, and the **capital market** for **long-term** investing and capital building. The capital market has two parts: the **primary market** (new issues) and the **secondary market** (stock exchange trading).

blocks.title: Money market vs capital market
rows: Low risk, high liquidity, lower yield

blocks.phrase: Money = Minutes to months (under a year). Capital = Calendar years (long term).
letters: Short term, less than one year, low yield
Long term, shares and bonds, higher return
blocks.note: Seven markets are covered in this chapter: money, capital, banking, pension, insurance, forex and commodity.

blocks.text: The **money market** trades securities with a **short maturity of less than one year**. These are often risk-free. Because maturity is short (high **liquidity**) and the risk of loss (volatility) is low, their **yield is also low**. An ordinary investor typically enters through **money market mutual funds**.

blocks.title: Money market securities
rows: Treasury bills: short-term government securities, original maturity under one year.
Repurchase agreement, a short-term borrowing instrument.

blocks.title: What is STT?
rows: A tax levied on all transactions done on stock exchanges, at rates prescribed by the Central Government from time to time.
The Government of India notified the **Securities Transaction Tax Rules, 2004**.

blocks.title: Mutual funds are not a money market instrument
blocks.text: **T-bills, CDs, CPs and Repo** are money market securities. A general mutual fund is a way to invest, not a money market security; only money market mutual funds are a route into the money market.

blocks.title: Money market instruments: T-C-C-R
blocks.note: All of them mature in less than a year.

blocks.text: Indian households have small savings, while companies need funds for their capital needs. A household can invest in business through the capital market (stock market) by buying **stocks and bonds**. Investors are either **retail** (individuals investing in personal capacity) or **institutional** (companies, banks, government, mutual funds, insurance and pension trusts). The **company** is the issuer and the source of demand for capital.

blocks.text: The **banking system** is part of the financial market. It consists of commercial banks, co-operative banks, payment banks, small finance banks and more, all regulated by the **Reserve Bank of India**. Banks collect deposits from the public (lenders with surplus money) and give credit as loans to individuals and companies. In this role the bank acts as an **intermediary**, and checks the borrower’s **credit worthiness** before it disburses a loan.

blocks.title: Pension market
blocks.text: The **pension market** serves the elderly with securities designed for them. Most Indians still do not get retirement benefits. Government and private sector employees are covered by **NPS, EPF or PPF**, but most self-employed people are not. The pension market aims to bring even them in. Products include NPS, PPF, retirement plans of insurance companies and mutual funds, and **EPFO**.

blocks.title: Insurance market
rows: Three product types: traditional products (term plans, endowment policies, whole life plans), variable products and unit-linked products. They give risk protection and investment benefits.
Motor insurance, health insurance, fire insurance and personal accident cover.

blocks.text: Insurance penetration in India is small. Many buy life insurance for **tax benefits** and motor insurance because it is **compulsory**. The market is growing with financial literacy and rising purchasing power, and medical, motor and term products are in demand.

The **forex market** is an online place where currencies are traded. It is the **most liquid** market of all, which is why traders and speculators like it. People trade because exchange rates keep changing and they want to profit from the movement. Every country has its own forex market, and all of them are linked online into one giant, **decentralised global forex market**.

blocks.title: Forex in India
items: Indian law permits forex trading **only in currency derivatives**.
**RBI and SEBI** strictly control trading in foreign currencies, so forex trading is less popular than the stock market or money market.
Currency pairs available for derivative trading: **USD-INR, EUR-INR, GBP-INR and JPY-INR**.
Currency trading is allowed on **NSE, BSE** and other exchanges such as MSEI.

To trade, one must open an account with a **broker permitted** to trade currency derivatives, such as Angel Broking, Axis Bank, Bajaj Financial Securities, Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, ICICI Bank and HDFC Bank.

blocks.title: Who regulates commodity trading?
blocks.text: Commodity futures were once regulated by the **Forward Markets Commission (FMC)**. FMC was merged into **SEBI in 2015**, so SEBI now regulates commodity derivatives. Older exam questions may still show FMC as the answer.

A customised, privately agreed contract for a future date.

rows: The difference in value between a country’s **exports and imports** of goods.

blocks.title: Option vs future
blocks.text: An **option** is a right, so the buyer can walk away. A **future** is an obligation for both sides. When the question says “right but not obligation”, think option.

A **Government Security (G-Sec)** is a tradable instrument issued by the **Central Government** or a **State Government**. It acknowledges the government’s debt. G-Secs carry practically **no risk of default**, so they are called **risk-free gilt-edged instruments**.

blocks.title: Short term and long term G-Secs
Types of government bonds
rows: Coupon rate stays fixed for the whole life of the bond until maturity.
No fixed coupon rate; first issued in India in **September 1995**.
Principal is linked to an accepted inflation index to protect the investor’s principal.

Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities: cash flows of a regular G-Sec (each semi-annual coupon and the final principal) are separated into individual securities. They are essentially zero coupon bonds.
Both coupon flows and principal are protected against inflation, using the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) or Consumer Price Index (CPI).

blocks.title: Who issues what
blocks.text: The **Centre** issues both T-bills and dated securities. **States** issue only dated securities, called **SDLs**.

blocks.title: Three ways of trading G-Secs in the secondary market
rows: Negotiated Dealing System, Order Matching. An order-driven electronic system where participants trade **anonymously** by placing orders or accepting others’. RBI introduced this screen-based module in **August 2005**.
A participant contacts a bank, primary dealer or financial institution directly or through a broker and negotiates price and quantity by phone. A deal is struck if both sides agree.

Launched by RBI on **29 June 2012**. Lets **gilt account holders (GAH)** take part in NDS-OM directly through their **primary members (PM)**. The PM acts only as a risk controller with no role in pricing.

blocks.text: The regulation of the Indian financial market is **top-down**. It starts with the **Ministry of Finance**, headed by the Finance Minister, and the following regulators work under it.

blocks.title: Regulation of the financial market
items: Banks, monetary, forex and credit policy

blocks.title: Regulators and their work
rows: Makes and regulates **monetary, forex and credit policies** and regulates all banks. This controls the supply of money and credit and influences interest rates on deposits and loans.
Securities and Exchange Board of India: the main regulator of the **primary and secondary markets** (stock exchanges).

Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India: regulates insurance, licenses insurers and regulates how insurance funds are invested. As per the syllabus it also oversaw the Tariff Advisory Committee for general insurance pricing.

Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority: regulates the pension sector, designed pension products such as NPS, decided NPS’s constituents and registers pension fund participants (custodians, CRA, trustee bank, fund managers).

blocks.title: FIMMDA
rows: Fixed Income Money Market and Derivatives Association of India.
Incorporated as a company under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956 on **3 June 1998**.

Scheduled commercial banks, public financial institutions, primary dealers and insurance companies, for example SBI, ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, Bank of America, Citibank, IDFC, EXIM Bank, NABARD, LIC and ICICI Prudential Life.
A **voluntary** market body for the bond, money and derivatives markets.
Represents members, acts as an **interface with regulators**, and develops the market, for example by introducing **benchmark rates** and new derivative instruments.
